content_html_sanitized:
NEW YORK
Richard N. Gottfried, chair of the New York State Assembly Committee on Health said that "thousands of New Yorkers with serious or life-threatening medical conditions," would benefit from medical cannabis. He spoke Wednesday at a New York State Bar Association briefing here on the legal implications of medicinal use of cannabis.

Gottfried recently introduced New York State legislation to allow physician-supervised use of marijuana to treat patients with serious illnesses. "I'm not saying it should be legalized or that marijuana abuse isn't a problem, only that it can have legal medical uses," he explained

Gottfried pointed out that, "if you take this artificial pill (Marinol) which has some stuff around the active ingredient, no problem. But if you inhale the natural form (of marijuana), the police can break down your door and cart you away. That, to me, is nuts!"

Dr. Robert B. Millman, acting chair of New York Hospital's Department of Public Health, told the briefing that much "anecdotal evidence" supports the medical use of marijuana to relieve nausea and vomiting associated with chemotherapy, increase appetite and well-being in wasting syndromes, and improve quality of life in people with seizure disorders, multiple sclerosis, chronic pain, and glaucoma.

Unfortunately, Dr. Millman went on to parrot the DEA party line saying, that in the last decade marijuana potency increased dramatically in New York City, from "1-2% maximum THC to 6-8%." This can make the difference, he said, "between being a little high and losing touch with reality." In fact, the average potency of marijuana as measured by the Federal government has not changed at all in the last decade, or the last two decades, for that matter. Moreover, there are no meaningful numbers for New York City contraband. Nor is there any evidence to support his claims on "losing touch with reality" – except for the mayor.

However, by saying this, he probably enhanced his credibility with the politicians. Of course, they will just quote him as an authority on the potency -- and then vote against the bill – because "marijuana is now so much more dangerous than it was back in the '60s – when we all thought that it was harmless."

To his credit, Dr. Millman did recognize that this had nothing to do with the medical use of marijuana, saying that if people with chronic diseases are left to fend for themselves, they may put themselves at risk for bacterial and pulmonary illnesses from contaminated street drugs. He added that that medicalization would also facilitate appropriately supervised medical research into the drug's benefits and risks. Of course, this is precisely why the DEA and HHS must stop medical marijuana at all costs and why they have blocked research for years.

Gottfried has introduced legislation calling for a monitoring system similar to those used for other controlled substances, including state monitoring of physician certifications to prevent abuse, state monitoring of nonprofit providers of marijuana solely for medical use, and periodic review and analysis by the Health Department. As with Proposition 215 in California, this will have no effect on Federal law, but it will add to the pressure on the DEA and HHS, who will put pressure on the state Assembly to vote against it.
